questiontext.text: How does the Decorator pattern add responsibilities to an object?

answer.text: Dynamically, by wrapping the object in a decorator at runtime

feedback.text: Correct — Decorator attaches responsibilities dynamically by wrapping.

answer.text: By ensuring only one shared instance exists

feedback.text: That describes Singleton, not Decorator.

answer.text: By composing objects into a part-whole tree

feedback.text: That describes Composite, not Decorator.

answer.text: By letting subclasses decide which product to create

feedback.text: That describes Factory Method, not Decorator.

generalfeedback.text: Decorator attaches additional responsibilities to an object dynamically by wrapping it in a decorator that shares the same interface.

questiontext.text: What does a decorator share with the component it wraps?

feedback.text: Correct — sharing the interface lets a decorator stand in for the component.
No — that is Singleton.
No — that is Builder.

generalfeedback.text: A decorator implements the same interface as the wrapped component, so clients cannot tell them apart.

questiontext.text: Decorator is often described as a flexible alternative to what?

feedback.text: Correct — Decorator adds behavior without a subclass explosion.
No — that is Singleton's concern.
No — that is Adapter's concern.

generalfeedback.text: Decorator provides a flexible alternative to subclassing for extending an object's behavior.

answer.text: Yes — multiple decorators can be stacked to combine behaviors

feedback.text: Correct — because each decorator wraps the same interface, they nest.

answer.text: No — only one decorator may ever wrap a component

feedback.text: No — stacking multiple decorators is a key strength.

answer.text: No — decorators must replace the component entirely

feedback.text: No — a decorator wraps rather than replaces the component.

generalfeedback.text: Since decorators share the component interface, they can be nested/stacked to accumulate responsibilities.

questiontext.text: Which statements about Decorator are true? (select all that apply)

answer.text: It attaches additional responsibilities to an object at runtime

feedback.text: Yes — that is Decorator's defining feature.

answer.text: A decorator implements the same interface as the component it wraps

feedback.text: Yes — this is what makes decorators transparent to clients.

answer.text: Its main purpose is to ensure a class has exactly one instance

feedback.text: No — that is Singleton.

answer.text: It requires a separate subclass for every combination of features

feedback.text: No — avoiding that subclass explosion is a reason to use Decorator.

generalfeedback.text: Decorator dynamically wraps a component sharing its interface, giving a flexible, stackable alternative to subclassing.

questiontext.text: Multiple decorators can be stacked to combine several added behaviors.

feedback.text: Correct — decorators nest because they share the component interface.
Stacking decorators to combine behaviors is a defining strength of the pattern.

questiontext.text: A decorator must expose a different interface than the object it wraps.

feedback.text: No — a decorator shares the same interface so it can transparently replace the component.
Correct — the decorator implements the same interface as the wrapped component.

questiontext.text: The structural pattern that attaches responsibilities to an object dynamically by wrapping it in an object of the same interface is the ______ pattern.

feedback.text: Correct.
Accepted — a decorator is a kind of wrapper.
Correct.
